prize_parts.citation: for the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development to 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Reading the eight opening ballots, the optical lattice clock is the candidate where the most colleagues independently reach the same configuration: Kroll and Lindroth rank it first, Mehlig second, and every member who ranked it proposed exactly Katori and Ye. As an instrument builder I judge it on the things I look for in a measurement prize. There is a clear original idea (magic-wavelength trapping, Katori), a decisive experimental development that took it to a quantitative frontier (Ye, with systematic uncertainty and stability at the 10^-18 level), and independent reproduction in several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) with intercontinental comparisons that agree. The physics will last: tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches, relativistic geodesy at millimetre scales, and a likely redefinition of the second. It is the patient calibration-and-systematics kind of work that I respect, and the two-person attribution is the cleanest of any shortlisted ballot. I am therefore moving my preferred configuration from my own first choice (B013) to B029, because on the evidence of the full committee it is the stronger and more defensible prize, and my role as Chair is to find a configuration the committee can stand behind.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control and ion clocks) already cover much of the precision-spectroscopy territory, and the committee could judge that a lattice clock is an evolutionary step rather than a new discovery. Olsson ranks it last of her eight and notes the direct benefit to humanity is currently modest, and it is true that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. There is also a real attribution question: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemke and others made key contributions to the 10^-18 milestone, and Ye's JILA record rests on a team. If the committee prefers a clear discovery of nature to a measurement advance, B013 or B031 would be the natural alternatives.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a field-opening measurement advance with a clear metric, multiple independent labs reproducing the performance, and a clean two-laureate configuration, while noting overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll on the metric and the reproduction, and that is what moves me. On overlap I would go slightly further: the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single ions; neither delivered thousands of atoms in a lattice at a magic wavelength reaching 10^-18 stability and systematic uncertainty. That is a distinct achievement. Where I would qualify Kroll is on Ye's role. I would want the citation to be phrased around the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, not a general 'precision clocks' wording, so that the ion-clock and comb work already honoured is not implicitly re-awarded.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B029 last of her eight, accepting that the clock is a verified measurement tool but doubting that the committee will see it as sufficiently distinct from 2005 and 2012 and noting that its benefit to humanity is currently modest; her first choice is NV-centre spin control and sensing (B001).
responses.response: I take the 'modest benefit' point seriously, but I disagree that it should decide the matter. Basic measurement advances routinely pay off in ways nobody predicts, and this one already has concrete outputs: international clock comparisons, relativistic geodesy and constraints on varying constants. On B001 I share her respect for NV centres as a measurement-driven tool, but I find the discovery boundary there less clear: single-centre optical detection, coherent control, nuclear-spin registers and the later sensing applications are different achievements, Hanson, Awschalom and others have strong claims, and Wrachtrup appears under overlapping candidates. That makes the attribution harder to defend than for the clock, where Katori's proposal and Ye's realisation line up neatly. I would keep B001 in view but not above B029.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a theory prediction followed by a decisive experiment producing a new quantum behaviour in a material, and ranks topological insulators second, while noting the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated.
responses.response: This is the competing configuration I take most seriously, and I am explicit that condensed matter is outside my expertise, so I rely on Eriksson and Mehlig for the physics. What I can weigh is the experimental maturity: the correlated and superconducting phases were reproduced by several groups quickly, which is encouraging, but by his own account the mechanism is unresolved and the field is under a decade old. My question is whether the credited contribution is settled enough to last, and whether we can defend giving three names (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) when Cao, Fatemi and other early experimentalists, and Dean's group on the hBN-encapsulated devices, also have claims. I would rather see B031 after the mechanism has clarified than gamble on it now, but I am prepared to be convinced if the condensed-matter members argue the flat-band picture is already the durable result.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs discovery through ATLAS and CMS first as an overdue, fully confirmed completion of the Standard Model and the experimental counterpart of the 2013 prize, but questions whether honouring experiment leadership rather than the discovery itself is right.
responses.response: I ranked B012 third myself and I share Ulf's view that the physics is beyond doubt. But I disagree with the idea that detector building is the obvious route to recognition here. I said in my opening that the instrument achievement deserves recognition, but the committee would be crediting three spokespersons or conceivers out of thousands, with the accelerator builders and other collaboration leaders left out, and the 2013 prize already honoured the discovery as such. As a detector builder I am especially wary: a prize that is read as 'the leaders of the collaboration' will be contested for years, and I do not think it is stronger than a clean two-person measurement prize. I would keep it as a fallback, not as the preferred configuration.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first, stressing the magic-wavelength idea, 10^-18 uncertainties confirmed by several laboratories, relativistic redshift over millimetres and redefinition of the second, with an unresolved question about fair division with ion-clock and frequency-comb work.
responses.response: Lindroth, as the atomic physicist, is best placed to say whether Katori and Ye hold the correct credit. I would ask her directly whether she believes the proposal history (Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength scheme, with Lemonde, Peik and others on the proposal side) is adequately represented by the two names. If she and Kroll think so, I am comfortable. I also agree with her that recognition is timely, since the independent comparisons at 10^-18 are in place.

uncertainties: Whether the proposal history (Lemonde, Peik, Hollberg and others) and the team contributions to the 10^-18 milestone (Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemke) are adequately captured by crediting only Katori and Ye.
Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 precision-measurement prizes.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene (B031) is mature enough, which depends on condensed-matter judgements I leave to Eriksson and Mehlig.
I have not independently verified exact priority dates and roles for B013, which remains my own alternative, and I have not checked whether the redefinition of the second will be decided soon.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred B029 configuration: I have no known personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or their groups. For disclosure, my own work in gamma-ray astronomy and polarimetry (Fermi-LAT, PAMELA, XL-Calibur) is adjacent to B013, my alternative, and to B037 in astroparticle physics, so I would weigh recusal on those if they were to become decisive, although I know none of their credited names as collaborators.
